key_terms.meaning: The right-hand side in a right sentential form that can be reduced to reverse one step of a rightmost derivation.
Reducing handles from right to left to build the reverse of a rightmost derivation.
A bottom-up parser with a stack and input; it shifts tokens or reduces a handle.
A stack prefix that can appear on the stack of a shift-reduce parser without error.
A sentential form reached by a rightmost derivation; the parser stack plus remaining input.
A production with a dot showing how much of its right side is already on the stack.
The set of items added to an LR item set by expanding nonterminals after the dot.
The transition from an item set on a grammar symbol to the item set after moving the dot over that symbol.
An LR(0) table whose reduce entries are placed only under terminals in FOLLOW of the left-hand side.
The terminals that can appear immediately after a nonterminal in some sentential form.
A table cell that asks for both a shift and a reduce.
A table cell that asks for two different reductions.
An LR(0) item plus one lookahead terminal that may follow the production.
The input terminal that decides whether a reduce action is allowed.
A state formed by merging LR(1) states with the same LR(0) core.
The set of LR(0) items in an LR(1) state, with lookaheads removed.
An LR parser whose states merge LR(1) states with the same core and keep combined lookaheads.
A parser generator that reads a grammar and actions and writes a C parser using LALR tables.
C code attached to a grammar rule and run when that rule is reduced.
A YACC declaration that sets the priority of operators and resolves some conflicts.

takeaways: Bottom-up parsing reduces handles to build a parse tree from leaves to root.
The stack plus input is a right sentential form; a correct reduction keeps a viable prefix.
LR(0) items and goto build a finite automaton that records possible parser stack states.
SLR uses FOLLOW to limit reductions, but FOLLOW is too coarse for some grammars.
Canonical LR(1) adds exact lookaheads and removes many conflicts at the cost of large tables.
LALR merges same-core LR(1) states, giving small tables and most of CLR power.
YACC turns an LALR grammar into a C parser and resolves conflicts using precedence or default choices.
Conflict reports matter: default shift or an earlier rule can hide a grammar error.
bank_note: Long answers usually demand a full item-set and table construction, a clear conflict diagnosis, and a comparison of SLR, CLR and LALR with YACC as the practical tool.

bank.q: Define a handle and explain handle pruning in shift-reduce parsing with a small grammar. Show the stack and input at each step.
Explain LR(0) items, closure and goto. Show how they build the LR(0) automaton for a given grammar.
Explain how SLR parsing tables are built. State exactly where shift and reduce entries go and why FOLLOW is used.
Describe the three sections of a YACC specification and explain how YACC produces a C parser from them.
For grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → ( E ) | id, build the LR(0) item sets and the SLR table. Mark any conflicts.
For a grammar with a shift-reduce conflict under SLR, construct canonical LR(1) items and the CLR table. Show whether the conflict disappears.
Merge LR(1) states with the same core and build the LALR table for a small grammar. Show the merged lookaheads.
Write a YACC specification for arithmetic expressions with +, *, parentheses and id. Add precedence and associativity declarations and explain each action.
Given a shift-reduce parser stack and input, decide the next move at each step using a handle. Identify an error step if one occurs.
Compare SLR, canonical LR(1) and LALR parsers in table size, lookahead precision and conflict behaviour. Give one grammar where they differ.
LALR merging can create a reduce-reduce conflict that canonical LR(1) does not have. Explain why with a grammar example and judge whether the smaller table is worth it.
A parser generator reports a shift-reduce conflict. Evaluate resolving it by precedence declarations, by grammar rewriting, and by accepting the default shift.
Trace how lookahead information moves from SLR to CLR to LALR. Explain which conflicts each stage removes or introduces.

glossary.def: A right-hand side that can be reduced to reverse one step of a rightmost derivation.
The process of repeatedly reducing handles to build a rightmost derivation backwards.
A bottom-up parser that uses a stack and chooses between shifting the next token and reducing a handle.
A prefix of a right sentential form that can appear on a shift-reduce parser stack without immediate error.
A derivation in which the rightmost nonterminal is expanded at every step.
A production with a dot marking the position reached by the parser.
The operation that adds items for productions of a nonterminal that appears just after the dot.
The operation that moves the dot over a grammar symbol and gives the next item set.
An item in a state that is not added by closure, such as the initial item or an item reached by goto.
An item added to a state by closure because a nonterminal follows the dot.
An LR parser that uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW sets to decide reduce actions.
The set of terminals that can come immediately after a nonterminal in some sentential form.
A table of shift, reduce, goto and accept actions that drives an LR parser.
A parse table cell that contains both a shift action and a reduce action.
A parse table cell that contains two different reduce actions.
An item with one terminal lookahead that may follow the production when it is reduced.
A terminal examined by the parser before choosing a reduce action.
An LR parser built by merging LR(1) states that have the same LR(0) core.
The LR(0) items of an LR(1) state, ignoring their lookaheads.
A parser generator that reads a grammar with actions and writes a C parser using LALR tables.
Code attached to a grammar rule that runs when the parser reduces that rule.
A YACC statement that assigns priority and associativity to operators to resolve conflicts.
A tool that reads a grammar specification and writes parser source code.
A grammar with a new start symbol and production that helps the parser detect acceptance.
